transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you. Well, what brings me in... I suppose for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around. Fixing things, arranging the living room, or volunteering for just one more thing. 

I volunteer down at the church, you see, organizing the charity drives. Oh, the amount of old coats people bring in! Last winter, someone donated a beautiful vintage mink—well, faux mink, I think—but the lining was completely torn. I used to sew quite a bit when I was younger, took a few home economics classes back in college before I met my husband, so I thought, 'I can fix that!' I spent three days driving around looking for the right thread. The traffic over by that craft store on Route 9 is just terrible lately, they've been doing all that construction on the overpass since April and it backs up all the way to the diner... 

But, oh, what was I saying? Right, right. It's just that, well, even at 87 years old, I have a very hard time just sitting down and being still. I just always have to be doing something.
Do you find that you have been having more trouble with your memory or your ability to keep track of things compared to how you were a few years ago?

Memory? Oh, no, my memory is sharp as a tack. I haven't noticed any trouble keeping track of things at all. Just the other day I remembered my neighbor Susan's birthday—she just turned 82, you know. I decided to bake her a cake, a lemon chiffon cake. My mother used to make those every Easter. 

Easter was so lovely back then, we'd all get dressed up in our Sunday best, the little white gloves... you just don't see people wearing gloves anymore. It's a shame, really. I saw a young woman at the grocery store last week wearing pajama bottoms! Can you imagine? At the grocery store! It was the one over on Elm Street, it used to be an A&P but they bought it out years ago. The produce manager there, Frank, he always saves the good tomatoes for me because he knows I like to make my own sauce. He has a daughter who just went off to college in Ohio, such a smart girl... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my memory. No, no, my mind is perfectly clear, I just can't seem to sit still in one place!
Have you noticed any periods, lasting a few days or longer, where you felt unusually energetic, talkative, or euphoric, perhaps needing much less sleep than usual?

Unusually energetic? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't get those wild bursts where I don't sleep. I sleep just fine, usually in bed by 10, right after I watch the evening news. Though, I have to say, the news these days is just so depressing. It's always one tragedy after another. 

Just last night they were talking about that terrible storm down in Florida. It reminded me of the hurricane we had back in '85. Gloria, I think it was. Oh, the wind! It knocked down the big oak tree in our front yard. My husband, God rest his soul, was so upset because he had planted that tree when we first bought the house in 1960. It was just a little sapling then, and it grew so beautifully. We had a swing hanging from one of the branches for the kids. My son, David, he used to swing on that thing for hours. He's a lawyer now, you know, lives out in Seattle. It rains so much out there, I don't know how he stands it. I always tell him he should move back East, but he says he loves the mountains. 

But, oh, what were we talking about? Sleep? Yes, I sleep my normal seven or eight hours. I just wake up and immediately feel like I need to be doing something, moving around. But no, no strange euphoric days or anything like that. Just my usual busy self.
When you feel like you have to be doing something, do you find that your mind is often filled with worries or concerns about things that might go wrong?

Worries? Oh, goodness, no. I wouldn't say I'm sitting around worrying about things going wrong. I just have this... this urge to keep busy. Like yesterday, I decided to clean out the hall closet. It's one of those deep closets, you know, where things just seem to disappear into the back. 

I found a whole box of old photographs in there! Pictures from our trip to the Grand Canyon in 1972. We drove the whole way in a station wagon, a big green Ford Country Squire with the fake wood paneling on the side. Oh, the kids hated being cooped up in the back seat for that long. My daughter, Sarah, she complained the entire time through New Mexico because the air conditioning couldn't keep up with the heat. She was always so particular about being comfortable. She’s an interior decorator now in Chicago, does these beautiful modern apartments, though I tell her they always look a little too cold for my taste. I like a house to feel lived in, you know? With comfortable chairs and maybe some nice floral curtains. I found some lovely fabric on sale at Joanne's last month, a yellow chintz...

Oh, dear, I'm wandering again, aren't I? What was the question? Worries? No, no, my mind isn't filled with worries. I just feel like there's always a project to do or something to fix!

When you feel this strong urge to be busy, do you feel any physical discomfort in your body, like a sense of restlessness in your legs or a feeling of being 'keyed up' or physically uneasy if you try to stop?

Physical discomfort? Well, I suppose you could call it that... it's more like this ants-in-my-chair feeling. Like when I'm at the senior center meetings, or sitting through those endless announcements at church. I just have to shift around, or stand up to get a coffee, or start straightening the papers on the table just to get through it. 

Speaking of the senior center, they just got a new coffee machine. One of those fancy ones where you put the little plastic cups in? Keurig, I think they call it. I don't care for it, honestly. The coffee always tastes a little bit like plastic to me. I prefer a traditional percolator. My grandmother had a beautiful stovetop percolator, enamel, bright red. She used to make coffee for my grandfather every morning at 5 AM before he went to work at the mill. He worked there for forty years, never missed a day. They don't make men like that anymore, do they? So dedicated. He used to bring home these little wooden spools for me to play with...

Oh, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? The keyed up feeling? Yes, yes, if I try to just sit still during those long meetings, I just feel like I have to move my legs or get up and do something.
Does this uncomfortable feeling in your legs happen primarily when you are lying down or trying to rest in the evening or at night, rather than just when you are sitting during the day?

At night? Oh, no, not really. When I get to bed, I'm usually tired enough to just go right to sleep. It's more during the day, like I said, when I'm stuck sitting somewhere. 

My evening routine is very settled, you see. I always have a cup of chamomile tea—just plain chamomile, none of those fancy blends with vanilla or lavender. I tried a lavender tea once that my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, brought over. She's always trying new things, that woman. Last week she took up water aerobics at the YMCA, and she's 82! Good for her, I suppose, but she slipped by the pool and bruised her hip. I told her she needs to be careful, the tiles get so slippery. We had a beautiful tile floor in our kitchen back in the 70s, a sort of mustard yellow. It was very popular at the time, but impossible to keep clean. Every little spill showed up... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the evening. No, I don't get that squirmy feeling in my legs when I'm trying to sleep, just when I'm sitting around during the day with nothing to do.

When you are working on your projects or tasks, do you find that you frequently jump from one thing to another before finishing the first, or do you find that you easily get distracted by other things you notice while you're busy?

Jump from one thing to another? Well, I don't... I mean, I suppose I get things done eventually. But it's just that there's always so much to see, you know? Like when I was cleaning that hall closet. I started taking the coats out to dust the shelf, and I noticed one of my late husband's old tweed jackets was missing a button. 

He loved that jacket. Wore it every autumn when we'd go apple picking up in upstate New York. We used to go to this wonderful little orchard, MacIntosh apples mostly, but they made the most incredible cider donuts. Hot, right out of the fryer, covered in cinnamon sugar. The line would be out the door of their little farm stand. My son, David, he could eat three of them in one sitting when he was a teenager. He always had such a sweet tooth. Still does, honestly, which is why his dentist is always scolding him. I told him he needs to use an electric toothbrush, they do a much better job than the manual ones. I bought one last year, a blue one, on sale at CVS... 

Oh, goodness, I've done it again, haven't I? Distracted. Yes, I suppose I do get distracted. I never did finish dusting that closet shelf, now that I think about it. I ended up looking for my sewing box to fix the button on the jacket, and then I found the photographs... so, yes, I suppose I do bounce around a bit.
Looking back at when you were a child or a teenager in school, did you often find it hard to stay focused on your lessons or feel like you had to be constantly moving around even back then?

School? Oh, goodness, that takes me back. Yes, I suppose I was always a bit of a handful, even in grade school. I remember the teachers were always scolding me because I'd just pop right out of my seat. I couldn't help it, I just had to be up and doing something. And I was always talking over the other children. They used to tell my mother I was 'too lively.' 

My mother, she was a saint, truly. She used to make all my clothes by hand. Beautiful little pinafores with smocking across the chest. You don't see smocking much anymore, do you? It takes such patience. She had this old Singer sewing machine, the kind with the foot treadle. It made the most rhythmic humming sound. I used to sit on the floor and watch her feet go back and forth, back and forth. Sometimes she'd let me sort her button tin. I loved that tin. It was an old Royal Dansk cookie tin—you know, the blue ones that always look like they have cookies in them but it's always sewing supplies? I bought one of those tins last Christmas for my grandson, hoping he'd like the cookies, but he's vegan now. Vegan! I don't know what he eats. No butter, no cheese... I make a wonderful macaroni and cheese, baked in the oven with a Ritz cracker crust. 

But, oh, I'm wandering again, aren't I? Yes, school. I was definitely 'too lively,' constantly moving and talking out of turn, long before I even reached high school.

patient.answer:
School? Oh, goodness, that takes me back. Yes, I suppose I was always a bit of a handful, even in grade school. I remember the teachers were always scolding me because I'd just pop right out of my seat. I couldn't help it, I just had to be up and doing something. And I was always talking over the other children. They used to tell my mother I was 'too lively.' 

My mother, she was a saint, truly. She used to make all my clothes by hand. Beautiful little pinafores with smocking across the chest. You don't see smocking much anymore, do you? It takes such patience. She had this old Singer sewing machine, the kind with the foot treadle. It made the most rhythmic humming sound. I used to sit on the floor and watch her feet go back and forth, back and forth. Sometimes she'd let me sort her button tin. I loved that tin. It was an old Royal Dansk cookie tin—you know, the blue ones that always look like they have cookies in them but it's always sewing supplies? I bought one of those tins last Christmas for my grandson, hoping he'd like the cookies, but he's vegan now. Vegan! I don't know what he eats. No butter, no cheese... I make a wonderful macaroni and cheese, baked in the oven with a Ritz cracker crust. 

But, oh, I'm wandering again, aren't I? Yes, school. I was definitely 'too lively,' constantly moving and talking out of turn, long before I even reached high school.

inference.note: The patient's report of lifelong symptoms of hyperactivity, impulsivity (talking over others), and distractibility (difficulty finishing tasks) starting in childhood strongly supports a diagnosis of ADHD, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive presentation, rather than an acquired condition like Restless Legs Syndrome (F48.8).

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the patient's primary reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation.
opening_question.question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of persistent inattention, distractibility, and motor restlessness (hyperactivity) that began in childhood and continues to cause functional interference in her daily activities. The symptoms are not better explained by restless legs syndrome (G25.81), as she explicitly denies nocturnal symptoms or discomfort specifically associated with rest/sleep, and they are not characteristic of a mood disorder.
